newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Clariden Bank favours European stocks over U.S..
newsitem.headline: Clariden Bank favours European stocks over U.S..

text.p: Beat Wittmann, chief investment officer for Clariden Bank, expects European stocks to outperform U.S. stocks in the next few years, but the trick for investors will be to pick the right individual stocks.
Wittmann said in an interview with Reuters that Clariden's current policy calls for a breakdown of 20 percent of assets in cash, 50 percent in bonds and 30 percent in equities.
"Right now, if you take the equity part, we are overweight in Europe, we are underweight in the U.S. and we are also underweight in Japan," Wittmann said.
Clariden, wholly-owned by Swiss financial group CS Holding, focuses solely on asset management, nearly exclusively for high-net worth individuals.
It has an estimated 10 billion Swiss francs under management, but does not publish assets, nor make public the number of its individual clients.
Wittmann said Clariden had changed its stance in July to more negative on the U.S. He expects a correction of perhaps 10 to 20 percent in the broad U.S. stock indices.
But he said the situation in European stocks could be compared to that in the U.S. market 10 years ago.
"We are very positive on Europe, not because it is very competitive, but because it is very uncompetitive," he said.
"Macro-wise, Europe is not interesting. It is really a corporate restructuring and growth story, on a company level," he said. There will be winners and losers, however.
"There are a lot of companies that will just go away. There are huge overcapacities, especially in banking and insurance," he said.
With respect to the U.S., Wittman said: "We think the U.S. market in terms of valuation is expensive, and we think the earnings momentum is peaking out."
Wittmann also expected the huge inflows of retail money into U.S. stocks to slow.
In Europe, however, he said that pension funds probably will put more money into stock markets.

"If I talk two to three years, the money will come mainly from European investors," he said. He estimated that the typical continental European pension fund was now invested at only around eight to 10 percent in equities, on average, but this would change.
"They need higher returns on their pension fund portfolios, therefore they need the higher equity component," he said.

With respect to individual stocks, Wittmann believes opportunities are offered in the growth category include French cosmetics firm L'Oreal. Swiss-based Nestle SA was an example of a more conservative growth stock.
He said German automaker Daimler Benz AG was an example of a restructuring stock.
But he cautioned that restructuring plays were hard to evaluate. "It is the management of change, which is very demanding. Management is the key to success," he said.
He said he would avoid any companies in which the state has an investment. This included many French companies.
Wittmann was also negative on an upcoming privatisation for Deutsche Telekom AG.
"We don't think the management can cut the fat to the extent there is any value for shareholders," Wittmann said.
He also said that impending European Monetary Union was likely to have little impact on stock markets.
"Monetary union is for me a non-issue in terms of impacts on these companies," he said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
